newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to try to cut 97/98 bond issue by 3 trln yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan to try to cut 97/98 bond issue by 3 trln yen.

text.p: Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Friday he and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto had agreed to work to reduce the government's planned bond issues for 1997/98 by more than three trillion yen.

"We will try to cut back on government bond issues by more than three trillion yen (in 1997/98). We will continue to cut bond issues beyond that year and will aim to balance expenditures excluding those related to bond repayments and tax revenues," Mitsuzuka told a news conference.

Japan plans to issue around 21 trillion yen worth of government bonds to finance its state budget for this fiscal year ending March 31, 1997. Of the 21 trillion yen, about 12 trillion yen will be deficit-financing bonds.

A MOF official told reporters separately that about 21.43 trillion yen worth of government bond issues would be needed to finance the 1997/98 state budget, judging from the compiled spending requests from various ministries.

According to the ministry's calculations, it sees 56.34 trillion yen worth of tax income and other revenue sources of 1.84 trillion yen in 1997/98. The imbalance would be made up by government bond issues to finance planned expenditures of 79.61 trillion yen, the MOF official said.
The MOF usually comes up with a draft budget by the end of December after much negotiation with other ministries, and it is submitted to the regular session of parliament in January for approval.
Mitsuzuka said the largest planned budget reduction in government bond issues was in 1981/82, when the government cut issues by two trillion yen.
But on an actual basis, the largest reduction was in 1988/89 when the bond issues were cut by 2.27 trillion yen.

Mitsuzuka said the three trillion yen worth of cuts in bond issues would centre on deficit-financing bonds. He said there was a need to review overall spending, especially that related to social security costs, such as medical insurance.
Mitsuzuka said the government has not made a final decision on whether to continue special income tax cuts next year, which are worth two trillion yen annually.
"But I think it is not appropriate to implement this (the special income tax cuts)," he said.
The economy is continuing to recover and tight fiscal finances will make it difficult to continue the cuts without issuing deficit-financing bonds, he said.

Asked about a report in a Japanese newspaper on Friday that the government and the Liberal Democratic Party had decided in principle to form a 1996/97 supplementary budget with economy boosting steps, Mitsuzuka said he knew nothing of such a decision.

"Although I don't think economic stimulative measures are necessary taking into account current economic conditions, we will consider what additional spending will be needed in the 1996/97 extra budget after grasping the overall situation," Mitsuzuka said.
